name: Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine

lead: Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine, sold as TriAsorB, is a newer triazine-class filter that its developers say covers UVB, UVA and high-energy blue light. It appeals to people worried about pigmentation and aging from sun and visible light.

Developer-authored papers describe it as a new-generation filter and report SPF50+ formulations containing it. Human studies are few and come largely from groups associated with its development; they examine blue-light-induced pigmentation and testing methods. The EU SCCS published a safety opinion in 2018.

paras: It is used as an ingredient in sunscreen formulations, often listed alongside bemotrizinol and tris-biphenyl triazine, as part of a daily SPF. Approval varies by jurisdiction.
No independent long-term human safety trials were found, and approval varies by jurisdiction.

chain: Absorbs UVB, UVA and blue light
angle.text: Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine (TriAsorB) is a newer filter its developers say covers UVB, UVA and high-energy blue light, which appeals to users worried about sun-driven pigmentation and aging. Studies so far come mostly from groups linked to its development.

lead: Phenylene bis-diphenyltriazine (PBDT), marketed as TriAsorB, is a synthetic organic sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB and UVA radiation and, according to its developers, also high-energy visible (blue) light.[1][2] It belongs to the triazine family of filters, alongside bemotrizinol and tris-biphenyl triazine.[3][4] Its appearance angle is photoprotection: sun exposure drives photoaging and uneven pigmentation, and a filter that also covers part of the visible spectrum is positioned as helping keep skin tone more even, particularly in people prone to dark marks.[2][5]

Developer-authored papers describe it as a new-generation filter with unusual optical properties and report SPF50+ formulations containing it.[1][2] The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety published an opinion on its safety under the code S86.[6] Most human data come from groups associated with its development and examine blue-light-induced pigmentation and testing methods.
infobox: UVB, UVA and blue light (per developers) [1]

paras: Sunscreen filters reduce ultraviolet damage that leads to wrinkling, loss of firmness, sunburn and tanning. Reviews of visible-light photoprotection report that high-energy visible light (blue light, roughly 400 to 490 nm) contributes to redness, persistent pigmentation and photoaging, with people with darker skin tones and certain light-sensitive skin conditions described as particularly susceptible.[7][8] Conventional UV-only sunscreens are described in these reviews as leaving visible light largely unaddressed, which is the gap that filters such as PBDT are designed to fill.[2][7]

In skincare communities the practical interest is in preventing hyperpigmentation such as melasma and post-inflammatory marks, which visible light can darken even when UV is blocked. A product containing the filter is used in the same way as other daily facial sunscreens.

The 2021 paper introducing the filter states that sunlight damage involves not only UV but also visible and infrared radiation through oxidative stress, and that balanced protection across the spectrum is therefore sought; the authors present PBDT, with CAS number 55514-22-2, as a filter designed for this purpose.[1] A 2022 paper describes formulating an SPF50+ sunscreen with it for protection against UVB, UVA and blue light.[2]

Separately, laboratory work using reconstructed human epidermis reported that blue light exposure reduced the repair rate of UVB-induced pyrimidine dimers, which authors cite as a rationale for blue light protection.[9] A 2022 imaging study formulated the filter with three other sunscreens and used mass-spectrometry imaging on human skin. It reported very low absorption, with most of the dose recovered on the surface, nothing entering the receptor fluid, and no increase in absorption in damaged skin.[10]

Bemotrizinol, sold as Tinosorb S, is a related triazine filter approved in the European Union since 2000 and, according to Wikipedia, approved for US sunscreens in June 2026.[4] Wikipedia's sunscreen article gives the general background on filter classes and how ingredient approval differs between regions.[3] PBDT does not have its own Wikipedia article.

The SCCS issued an opinion on the safety of the ingredient in 2018.[6] Review articles on visible light protection discuss it among emerging approaches, and approval status varies by jurisdiction.[3][7][8]

A 2023 paper evaluated nine PBDT-containing sunscreens in vitro for blue-light photostability and photoprotection, together with a clinical evaluation of blue-light-induced skin pigmentation.[5] A separate 2023 paper described an in vivo method for evaluating sunscreen protection against high-energy visible light using multispectral imaging of volunteers' forearms; it compared five SPF 50+ products with conventional organic filters, one product containing PBDT and a no-filter control.[11] Both come from the filter's development context and no independent long-term trials were found.

Visible-light and blue-light protection, particularly for hyperpigmentation, is discussed in skincare communities, and this filter is mentioned as one option marketed for that purpose. Community discussion of the filter itself is sparse.
